# Tax-Credit Zones: Enterprise Zones, Opportunity Zones & Rural Jump-Start

Some Colorado land sits inside zones where the state or federal government pays part of the cost of developing it,
or of running a business on it. This page explains the three programs that matter for buying and developing land,
then lists every county. Each [county page](counties/README.md) has a **Tax-credit zones** section with the
details: which zone, how much of the county it covers, which towns are in it, and each opportunity zone tract.

> **This is research, not tax advice.** The programs below are tax credits and deferrals with pre-certification
> steps, deadlines and recapture rules. Talk to a Colorado CPA before you count on any of them in a purchase price.

Checked 2026-09-30. Next review 2026-12-15: Treasury is expected to certify the OZ 2.0 tracts by the end of November 2026; re-check then.

## Which program fits which plan

| Your plan for the land | Program that can help | What it pays |
|---|---|---|
| Build or expand a business there (campground, farm stay, shop, workshop) | Enterprise zone | State income-tax credits on equipment, hiring, training and rehab |
| Rehab an old vacant commercial building | Enterprise zone | 25% of rehab costs, up to $50,000 in credits |
| Start a new business that sells outside the county and hires | Rural Jump-Start | 100% relief of state income and sales tax and county business personal property tax, plus a $15,000-$25,000 grant |
| Reinvest a capital gain (from stocks, a business or property sale) into development | Opportunity zone | Deferred tax on the gain, a basis step-up, and no tax on the new investment's growth after 10 years |
| Buy land and hold it | None | None of these programs pays for owning land without developing or using it |

## Enterprise zones (state)

Colorado has 16 enterprise zones, run by 19 local administrators, in areas with high unemployment, low income or
slow population growth. OEDIT redesignated every zone for **2026-01-01 to 2036-01-01**
([redesignation](https://oedit.colorado.gov/programs-and-funding/tax-credits/enterprise-zone-program/enterprise-zone-redesignation), [zone map layer](https://services3.arcgis.com/DgjqnJA1rgO92Soi/arcgis/rest/services/Enterprise_Zones/FeatureServer/2)). Businesses in a zone can earn state income-tax credits
([OEDIT program page](https://oedit.colorado.gov/enterprise-zone-program); [DOR credit guide](https://tax.colorado.gov/enterprise-zone-tax-guide)):

- **Investment tax credit:** 3% of business personal property (equipment, not land or buildings).
- **New employee credit:** $1,100 per net new employee, more in enhanced rural zones and for agricultural processors.
- **Employer health insurance credit:** $1,000 per net new insured employee, first two years.
- **Job training credit:** 12% of eligible training costs.
- **Vacant commercial building rehabilitation credit:** 25% of rehab costs for a commercial building at least 20 years old and vacant at least two years (up to $50,000 in credits).
- **Research and development credit:** 3% of the increase in R&D spending.
- **Commercial vehicle credit:** 1.5% of new commercial trucks and trailers.
- **Contribution projects:** anyone who donates to a certified local zone project gets a 25% credit on cash (12.5% in kind), up to $100,000 a year.

A business must **pre-certify** with its zone administrator through OEDIT's portal before the activity, every tax
year, then certify afterward and file the certificate with its Colorado return.

**Enhanced rural enterprise zones** (2025-2026) earn larger new-employee credits. They are Alamosa, Archuleta, Baca, Bent, Cheyenne, Clear Creek, Conejos, Costilla, Crowley, Custer, Delta, Dolores, Fremont, Hinsdale, Huerfano, Jackson, Kiowa, Kit Carson, Lake, Las Animas, Lincoln, Logan, Mineral, Moffat, Morgan, Otero, Phillips, Prowers, Rio Blanco, Rio Grande, Routt, Saguache, San Juan, Sedgwick, Washington, Yuma,
plus parts of Montrose and San Miguel (the Tier 1 coal transition areas only). OEDIT updates the list every two years.

## Opportunity zones (federal)

Opportunity zones are low-income census tracts where investing **capital gains** through a qualified opportunity fund
defers and reduces federal tax, and Colorado follows the federal treatment. There are two maps ([OEDIT](https://oedit.colorado.gov/colorado-opportunity-zone-program)):

- **Current map:** 126 tracts designated in 2018 ([HUD layer](https://services.arcgis.com/VTyQ9soqVukalItT/arcgis/rest/services/Opportunity_Zones/FeatureServer/13)), open for investment through **2028-12-31**.
  62 of them count as rural under the new definition ([IRS Notice 2025-50](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-drop/n-25-50.pdf)),
  so investments there now get the lower 50% improvement threshold.
- **2027 map:** H.R. 1 (July 2025) made the program permanent, with a new map every 10 years. Treasury found
  360 eligible tracts in Colorado in April 2026 ([list](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1RAYSjXre7xUF2cbpDGsukz9nroysvwce/edit)),
  then raised the count to 362, which set the 25% cap at 91. On 2026-09-28 the Governor nominated the maximum,
  **91**, including 28 rural ([press release](https://oedit.colorado.gov/press-release/fostering-economic-growth-polis-administration-submits-maximum-number-of-91)). The per-county eligible counts here come from the April list.
  Treasury is expected to certify them by the end of November 2026, and they open for investment on **2027-01-01**.
  See OEDIT's [OZ 2.0 GIS tool](https://experience.arcgis.com/experience/5f598808a6c240d7a7aa0adb2585316c) for the map.

Benefits under the 2027 rules ([OEDIT](https://oedit.colorado.gov/colorado-opportunity-zone-program); [EIG summary](https://eig.org/opportunity-zones-2-0-where-things-stand/)):

- **Deferral:** tax on the original gain is deferred for five years from the date of investment.
- **Step-up:** after five years, 10% of the deferred gain is forgiven, or **30%** through a qualified rural opportunity fund
  (at least 90% of its assets in rural tracts).
- **Exclusion:** hold the fund investment 10 years and its growth is tax-free (capped at 30 years).
- **Substantial improvement:** an existing building must be improved by 100% of its basis within 30 months, or **50%**
  in a rural tract.

**For land:** unimproved land in a zone doesn't itself have to be substantially improved, but land bought with no
expectation of improving it more than an insubstantial amount within 30 months fails the anti-abuse rule
([26 CFR 1.1400Z2(d)-2(b)(4)(iv)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/26/1.1400Z2(d)-2)). In practice the
fund has to build something, such as housing, cabins, a campground or a business, not hold the land.

## Rural Jump-Start (state)

For a **new** business in a participating distressed county that exports goods or services outside the county,
partners with a sponsoring college or economic development group, and hires 3-5 new full-time employees at the
county's average wage or more. It can't compete with an existing business in the county or a neighboring distressed
county. Benefits are 100% relief of state income tax, state sales and use tax, county (and participating
municipal) business personal property tax, and state income tax for qualified new hires, plus a matching grant
of up to $15,000, or $25,000 in Tier 1 coal transition communities. Tax benefits run through
2030-12-31 and grants through 2028-06-30 ([OEDIT](https://oedit.colorado.gov/rural-jump-start-program)).

- **Participating zones:** Alamosa, Archuleta, Clear Creek, Conejos, Costilla, Delta, Dolores, Fremont, Garfield, Huerfano, Kiowa, Kit Carson, La Plata, Lake, Las Animas, Lincoln, Logan, Mesa, Moffat, Montezuma, Montrose, Morgan, Otero, Phillips, Prowers, Pueblo, Rio Blanco, Rio Grande, Routt, Saguache, San Juan, Sedgwick, Washington, Yuma.
- **Eligible but not yet participating:** Baca, Bent, Cheyenne, Crowley, Custer, Hinsdale, Jackson, Mineral, Park.

## How this data is built

- `pipelines/incentives/programs.json`: hand-entered facts from the sources above (zone administrators, enhanced
  rural and Rural Jump-Start lists, nominated tracts), each with a source id.
- `pipelines/incentives/build.mjs`: downloads the zone and tract maps and Census 2020 town boundaries, measures the
  overlaps with mapshaper, and writes `pipelines/incentives/zones.json`.
- `pipelines/hosting/build.py`: renders this page, the section on each county page, and the county panel data.

```sh
node pipelines/incentives/build.mjs --refresh   # re-download the maps (after Treasury certifies the 2027 tracts, say)
python3 pipelines/hosting/build.py              # regenerate the wiki and app data
```
